young.html: John Stuart Mill was an English thinker who lived in the 1800s. His father taught him Greek when he was three! When he grew up, he wrote a small book with a big idea, called On Liberty.

Mill's idea is simple to say: you should be free to run your own life, as long as you are not harming other people. If what you do affects only you, other people may give you advice, but they should not force you. If what you do hurts someone else, then the community can step in.

Mill also thought people must be free to say what they think, even when most people disagree. Maybe the one person who disagrees is right! And even if they are wrong, arguing with them helps everyone understand the truth better.

young.name: gb-mill-harm
young.cap: Ten cases, all from Mill's own book. Decide what Mill would say, then see his reason.

young.html: Where is the line? Make two columns: "only affects me" and "affects other people." Sort these: what color socks you wear; playing loud music at midnight; eating your vegetables; borrowing a friend's bike without asking; reading a book everyone else thinks is boring. Were any hard to sort? Why?

full.html: John Stuart Mill (1806–1873) was raised by his father, the philosopher James Mill, in a famous experiment in education: Greek at three, Latin at eight, economics and logic before he was fourteen. At twenty he fell into a deep depression and found his way out partly through poetry, especially Wordsworth. He worked for the East India Company for thirty-five years, served one term in Parliament, and wrote on logic, economics, ethics and politics.
He planned On Liberty with Harriet Taylor, his close friend for twenty years and then his wife. She died in 1858; the book came out in 1859, dedicated to her memory.

full.text: That principle is, that the sole end for which mankind are warranted, individually or collectively, in interfering with the liberty of action of any of their number, is self-protection. That the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilised community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others. His own good, either physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant.
full.author: Mill
full.ed: John W. Parker and Son, London

full.html: Mill applies this only to adults "in the maturity of their faculties," not to children. And he worries about two kinds of control: laws, and the quieter pressure of public opinion and custom, which he calls a social tyranny that can be worse than many kinds of political oppression.

full.name: gb-mill-harm
full.cap: Mill's own cases, from the drunken policeman to the unsafe bridge.

full.text: If all mankind minus one, were of one opinion, and only one person were of the contrary opinion, mankind would be no more justified in silencing that one person, than he, if he had the power, would be justified in silencing mankind.
full.author: Mill
full.ed: John W. Parker and Son, London

items: The silenced opinion may be true. To silence it is to claim we cannot be wrong.
It may hold part of the truth, and the accepted view is rarely the whole of it.
Even a true belief, if never challenged, becomes a dead dogma, held without understanding.

full.html: Mill draws a line at incitement: the opinion that grain dealers starve the poor may be printed in a newspaper, but may be punished when it is shouted to an excited mob outside a grain dealer's house.

Chapter III praises individuality. Human nature, Mill writes, is not a machine built to a pattern but a tree that needs to grow on all sides. Society gains from "experiments of living," because no one knows in advance which ways of life will turn out best.

Critics, then and now, ask where "harm to others" begins. Almost anything a person does affects someone. Mill's early critic James Fitzjames Stephen (1873) argued that society has always rightly enforced some morals. Others say Mill underrates how much people need shared customs. Defenders answer that the principle is meant to put the burden of proof on anyone who wants to restrict liberty. The book is still at the center of these debates.

Reading Mill as saying "anything goes." He wanted people to advise, persuade and even avoid one another freely; what he opposed was force, by law or by social punishment, over acts that concern only oneself.

items: Milton's Areopagitica (1644) had argued for a free press: let truth and falsehood grapple.
Tocqueville's Democracy in America gave Mill the fear of a "tyranny of the majority"; Mill reviewed both volumes.
Mill's Utilitarianism, his next rung, rests liberty on the long-run happiness of humanity, not on natural rights, an argument critics have questioned ever since.
Humboldt, a German thinker, gave Mill the motto on his title page: the full development of each person in its richest diversity.
Is offending someone a kind of harm?
Should people be stopped from harming themselves? Always, never, or sometimes?
Can public opinion be a tyrant even when the law is fair?
What do you learn by hearing the best case for a view you reject?

questions: Can you think of something that only affects you? Is anything truly only about you?
Have you ever changed your mind after hearing someone disagree with you?
Mill thought being different helps everyone learn. Do you agree?
When should a parent step in to stop a child from a risk? When should they let the child decide?
Why might people be afraid to say what they think, even where the law allows it?
